question: A 4-week-old male infant is brought with forceful, non-bilious vomiting after every feed for the past 2 weeks. He appears hungry and feeds eagerly. A visible gastric peristalsis is noted on the abdomen. Which ONE statement BEST describes the next step?

answers.text: Reassure the mother — projectile vomiting is physiological at this age and resolves with time.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Projectile non-bilious vomiting with visible gastric peristalsis in a 4-week-old is the classic presentation of pyloric stenosis, not a normal variant. Reassurance without investigation is inappropriate.

answers.text: Order a bedside abdominal ultrasound to measure the pyloric muscle length and thickness.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is confirmed on ultrasound: pyloric muscle thickness ≥4 mm and channel length ≥14 mm are the diagnostic criteria. Ultrasound is the investigation of choice — fast, non-ionising, and highly accurate.

answers.text: Refer immediately for upper GI barium study because bilious vomiting demands urgent surgical evaluation.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect on two counts: (1) the vomiting described is NON-bilious — pyloric stenosis causes non-bilious vomiting since the obstruction is above the ampulla of Vater; and (2) ultrasound is preferred over barium study for pyloric stenosis.

answers.text: Start oral rehydration salts and observe for 48 hours before arranging any investigation.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Pyloric stenosis causes a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis from persistent vomiting. IV fluid resuscitation (not oral ORS) and prompt surgical referral for pyloromyotomy are required after confirmation on ultrasound.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the classification of vomiting by content and age. Bilious vomiting = surgical emergency; non-bilious projectile in a young infant with visible peristalsis = hypertrophic pyloric stenosis → ultrasound, then pyloromyotomy.

Well done. Pyloric stenosis (peak 2–6 weeks, males 4:1) classically presents with projectile non-bilious vomiting and a visible gastric peristaltic wave. Ultrasound is the gold-standard confirmatory test.
